questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of progressive dyspnea and a one-week history of fever, chills, and productive cough. The patient eventually required intubation and mechanical ventilation due to respiratory distress and hypoxemia. A chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the left and right lower lobes and patchy airspace opacity in the right middle lobe. Blood cultures were taken and empirical antimicrobials started.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate further investigation?

options.text: Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen assays
NAAT for Chlamydia and Mycoplasma pneumoniae on throat swab

questions.explanation: Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen assays The patient in this clinical vignette has presented with a severe pneumonia requiring admission to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. The recommendation for patients presenting with a severe community-acquired pneumonia is to have Legionella and S. pneumoniae urine antigen testing in addition to blood and sputum cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q13

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man was admitted with a 1-week history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, dry cough, fever, chills, and myalgia. He was beginning to feel better until 48 hours ago when he developed recurrence of fever and chills, a productive cough with blood-streaked sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. On physical examination, his temperature was 38.8°C, blood pressure 100/50 mmHg, pulse rate 110/minute, and respiration rate 24/minute. CXR: right middle lobe airspace disease with a small area of cavitation as well as blunting of the right costophrenic angle.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin This patient has a classic presentation for a postinfluenza or viral illness with initial flu-like symptoms progressing to worsening fever, productive cough, and imaging findings suggestive of a pleural effusion. Although the infection could be due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, there is concern for postinfluenza Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, and the patient requires empiric coverage for MRSA. Although daptomycin does provide MRSA coverage, it is inactivated in the lung by surfactant and would be a poor choice in this clinical scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q5

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with 3 days of fever and cough. She had no known allergies. On exam her temperature was 39.1°C. Investigations: CXR: patchy bilateral infiltrates
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin The patient presents in the setting of community-acquired pneumonia. The only answer choice with a guideline-recommended regimen for CAP is ceftriaxone and azithromycin. The patient has no past medical history or risk factors warranting pseudomonal coverage and does not present with evidence of a pleural effusion after a viral illness that would be concerning for MRSA infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q5

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman was diagnosed with healthcareassociated pneumonia. She was a nursing home resident with no drug allergies, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and acute on chronic kidney disease. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 25 mL/min (baseline creatinine clearance 40 mL/min) Sputum culture negative Multiplex PCR respiratory virus panel negative
questions.lead_in: What antipseudomonal agent poses the greatest risk for neurotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Cefepime While each of the beta-lactam antibiotics listed has the potential to cause neurotoxicity, cefepime is most associated with the development of this adverse effect. A US Food and Drug Administration safety alert for cefepime identified age >50 and inadequate renal dosing adjustments as risk factors for neurotoxicity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q4

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with a 2-day history of fever and chills, dyspnea, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Five months earlier she underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome. She was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, aciclovir, prednisone, and cyclosporine. Investigations: CXR: infiltrate in the left lower lobe
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae The patient is 5 months out from a stem cell transplant and presents with a lobar pneumonia. Although she is immunocompromised, she is on Pneumocystis prophylaxis and does not present with interstitial lung disease. CMV pneumonia would also be unlikely without a diffuse pneumonitis on imaging, and she would require histopathology with positive CMV staining to make the diagnosis. RSV pneumonia would normally present with bilateral asymmetric infiltrates and Candida spp. rarely cause pneumonia. The correct answer is therefore pneumococcal pneumonia as this patient is at risk for pneumococcal pneumonia, and a lower lobe infiltrate would fit the classic description.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q4

questions.question: 11. A patient is admitted with a community-acquired pneumonia. The culture reveals an MRSA, resistant to TMP-SMX and macrolides. The patient had an allergic reaction to vancomycin. He is started on daptomycin, but keeps worsening clinically.

parts.text: Why is he still worsening?
b) What are 2 antibiotics you could use in this particular scenario (assuming the organism is susceptible)?

cohort_answer.text: Daptomycin is not active in the lung (inactivated by pulmonary surfactant).

questions.question: Pneumonia (inpatient, mild) in a pregnant woman with SJ to PCN.

parts.text: What is your treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides are safe for pregnancy. UpToDate suggests: Clindamycin plus aztreonam for mild CAP requiring admission with contraindication to cephalosporins. Short course of Moxifloxacin should be fine (author's opinion). If severe: Vancomycin, aztreonam and azithromycin. (ATS 2001; note - avoid all beta-lactams if Stevens-Johnson syndrome.)

parts.text: A woman is 16 weeks pregnant. She is admitted for community acquired pneumonia. She has SJS to penicillin. She is tachypneic but otherwise stable. What is one empiric regimen that you would recommend to treat her pneumonia?

questions.model_answer: Empiric regimen: azithromycin monotherapy (500 mg IV/PO daily) - covers atypical pathogens and reasonable typical coverage, safe in pregnancy, and avoids penicillin/cephalosporin given SJS history (an absolute contraindication to beta-lactams, including cross-reactive cephalosporins); if additional gram-negative/typical coverage needed, a respiratory fluoroquinolone (e.g. levofloxacin) can be considered as an alternative, though generally avoided in pregnancy unless no other option, making azithromycin the preferred choice here.

questions.question: For the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: Retropharyngeal abscess on Peds exam, VAP on adult exam, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

parts.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

cohort_answer.text: Retropharyngeal abscess 14 days (UTD, Redbook); VAP 7 days; CAP 5 days; Cellulitis 5 days; Uncomplicated pyelo 7 days. Resource: AMMI Duration Paper https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9615468/

questions.question: Write the shortest duration of therapy for VAP, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated Pyelo

parts.text: VAP
CAP
Cellulitis
Uncomplicated Pyelonephritis

cohort_answer.text: VAP: 3 days (IDSA 2016). CAP: 3 days (IDSA 2019). Cellulitis: 5 days (IDSA 2014). Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (IDSA 2010; fluoroquinolones only for 5d if local resistance <10%).

questions.question: Based on the best available evidence, what is the shortest available duration of therapy for the following conditions, assuming clinical improvement and defervesced at 48 hours in each case on therapy?

parts.text: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E coli pyelonephritis without any stones or obstruction?
Klebsiella bacteremia due to a now-passed stone with no evidence of abscess or complication?
Fully-susceptible, pulmonary TB without dissemination?
Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removal, repeat blood cultures at 48 hours negative, TEE negative for IE, and no other signs of metastatic infection?
Community acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis not on oxygen?
Perforated diverticulitis status post OR for washout without any concern of residual abscess per the surgeon?

questions.model_answer: Shortest evidence-based durations: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E. coli pyelonephritis (no stones/obstruction) - 5 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); 7 days if using a beta-lactam or TMP-SMX. Klebsiella bacteremia from a passed stone, no abscess/complication - 7 days. Fully-susceptible pulmonary TB without dissemination - 6 months (2 months RIPE + 4 months INH/RIF), the shortest standard regimen. Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removed, negative repeat cultures at 48h, negative TEE, no metastatic infection - 14 days (uncomplicated bacteremia). Community-acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis, not on oxygen, afebrile by 48h - 5 days (minimum per IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP guideline). Perforated diverticulitis status post operative washout with adequate source control, no residual abscess - 4 days (per fixed-duration antibiotic data, e.g., STOP-IT trial approach).
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA/ATS CAP guideline (2019), STOP-IT trial (complicated intra-abdominal infection duration), and short-course gram-negative bacteremia trial data (e.g., Yahav et al. 2019) - not covered in this Mandell Staph aureus chapter.

questions.question: Curve which showed three curves representing different AUC/MIC ratios used, % of isolates remaining susceptible / days of clinical infection

parts.text: A. Asked to state which ratio (AUC/MIC < 100 or AUC/MIC >= 100) was represented by the bottom curve (in the graph below, the dotted curve) and explain.
B. Two classes of antimicrobials whose efficacy is predicted by AUC/MIC.
C. Three principles to reduce drug resistance when treating a patient with gram-negative pneumonia in ICU.

cohort_answer.text:
[image-based question: graph of AUC/MIC curves not otherwise described]. Concentration-Dependent Killing: rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; usually protein or DNA synthesis inhibitors e.g. Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin; exhibit post-antibiotic effect. Time-Dependent Killing: usually cell wall synthesis inhibitors e.g. Beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides, probably Vancomycin; bactericidal activity continues as long as plasma concentration > MIC
Glycopeptides; Tetracyclines; Oxazolidinones; Azithromycin; Triazoles; Clindamycin
Base choice of antibiotics on local antibiogram; Shorten duration - 5-7 days for VAP; Use therapeutic drug monitoring; Implement protocols. Additional: Empiric treatment informed by local antibiogram; dosing based on PK/PD data; definitive therapy based on susceptibility testing; optimize duration to 7 days; appropriate infection control practices

questions.question: 3 year old girl with URTI followed by fever and respiratory distress. CXR shows a large lobar consolidation and pleural effusion.

parts.text: A) List the 3 most likely organisms to cause this?
B) What other information do you want to know?
C) What is your treatment?
D) What other management might be helpful?

cohort_answer.text:
Streptococcus pneumoniae; Staphylococcus aureus; Group A streptococcus; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis
Vaccination status; recurrent sinopulmonary infections; close contacts (need for chemoprophylaxis); MRSA colonization rate (personal/family)
Amp or Cefotaxime/CTX based on local guidelines + Vanco if proven or severe suspected MRSA pneumonia
Drain pleural effusion to expedite resolution of symptoms and complex pneumonia
